article_title: SWIM: Student Writing Simulation via Proficiency-Conditioned Generation
citation: Heejin Do, Jakub Kontak, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). SWIM: Student Writing Simulation via Proficiency-Conditioned Generation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.03215. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03215
title: SWIM: proficiency-conditioned essay generation task with AES-based profile-alignment evaluation and the Proficiency Alignment Reward
description: SWIM formalizes student writing simulation as proficiency-conditioned essay generation: given a writing prompt and a target trait-score profile, a generator produces an essay exhibiting the specified writing behavior, and "an AES-based evaluation framework for" measuring profile alignment scores the output with a frozen multi-trait AES verifier using QWK. The authors train generators via SFT on real (essay, profile) pairs and then refine them with GRPO using the Proficiency Alignment Reward, a dense per-sample reward based on trait-normalized accuracy against the target profile.
requirements: A trait-score-annotated essay corpus with prompt-specific rubrics and score ranges, and a frozen multi-trait AES verifier as external evaluator
constraints: Evaluation relies on AES as a proxy for fidelity and cannot fully replace human judgment of authenticity
Experiments cover a limited set of writing prompts and proficiency distributions on ASAP/ASAP++
Static proficiency profiles do not model evolving learner states such as knowledge, motivation, or writing strategies over time
target_learners: simulated K-12 and secondary student writers across grade levels in the ASAP/ASAP++ corpus
target_learning_goals: reproducing multidimensional writing proficiency (content, organization, lexical choice, sentence fluency, conventions) at specified levels
examples: GRPO-trained Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct generated qualitatively distinct essays for ASAP Prompt 5 at target Overall scores 1/4, 2/4, and 4/4, with length and structural sophistication scaling with the requested level
key_sources: Heejin Do, Jakub Kontak, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). SWIM: Student Writing Simulation via Proficiency-Conditioned Generation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.03215. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03215

article_title: Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem
citation: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527
title: Swiss cheese model of trust calibration: layered interpretability affordances, engagement mechanisms, and literacy cover one another's gaps
description: The article borrows Reason's Swiss cheese model as its integrating frame: "every safety barrier has holes, yet stacked barriers rarely let a hazard through all of them at once." Interpretability affordances miss unmotivated users; engagement mechanisms catch them but may miss users whose checks are ineffective; literacy building closes gaps slowly but durably. A user who cannot evaluate citations may still be reached by a dialogue scaffold or a social signal, so layered combinations can make uncritical acceptance rare.
requirements: No single intervention can fully recalibrate user trust, so layers must be combined
constraints: Each layer's holes are located by the user typology, and literacy building works slowly
target_learners: All chatbot users across the four typology profiles
target_learning_goals: Reducing uncritical acceptance of chatbot outputs
examples: The COVID-19 pandemic publicized the model, where masks, ventilation, and vaccines were each imperfect and jointly effective
key_sources: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527

article_title: Effects of School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Child Behavior Problems
citation: Catherine P. Bradshaw, Tracy E. Waasdorp, Philip J. Leaf. (2012). Effects of School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Child Behavior Problems. Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2012-0243
title: SWPBIS as a 3-tiered universal prevention framework altering the school's organizational context
description: SWPBIS is a noncurricular universal prevention strategy that "aims to alter the school 's organizational context to implement enhanced procedures and systems to guide data-based decisions related to student behavior problems and academics." It applies behavioral, social learning, and organizational principles school-wide, establishes positively stated expectations taught to all students and staff, and implements "a 3-tiered prevention framework" in which selective and indicated programs complement universal components. In this trial it was delivered via team training, booster sessions, and monthly behavior-support coaching.
requirements: Schools form SWPBIS teams of 5 to 6 members who attend an initial 2-day summer training co-led by a developer and annual 2-day booster training events
At least monthly on-site support and technical assistance from a trained behavior support coach
constraints: Most of the more than 16,000 implementing schools have focused on the universal components rather than the full 3-tiered model
Some children do not respond adequately to the universal model
target_learners: Elementary school children (kindergarten through grade 2 cohorts in the trial)
target_learning_goals: Reducing aggressive and disruptive behavior
Improving prosocial behavior and emotion regulation
Reducing office discipline referrals
examples: In the 4-year group RCT, 21 schools received SWPBIS training and coaching led by the PBIS Maryland State Leadership Team while 16 comparison schools refrained from implementing SWPBIS for 4 years
key_sources: Catherine P. Bradshaw, Tracy E. Waasdorp, Philip J. Leaf. (2012). Effects of School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Child Behavior Problems. Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2012-0243

article_title: Examining variation in the impact of school-wide positive behavioral interventions and supports
citation: Bradshaw, C. P., Waasdorp, T. E., & Leaf, P. J. (2015). Examining Variation in the Impact of School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports: Findings From a Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037630
title: SWPBIS is a multitiered whole-school prevention framework aimed at altering the school environment
description: The article describes Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports as "a multitiered system o f supports framework aimed at altering the school environment through improved systems, data-based decision making, and implemention of evidence-based practices." It applies behavioral, social learning, and organizational principles across all school contexts to prevent disruptive behavior and enhance school climate. The model follows a three-tiered prevention model in which selective (Tier 2) and indicated (Tier 3) programs complement universal (Tier 1) school-wide components. Most of the more than 20,000 implementing schools focus on the universal elements due to resource needs.
requirements: Implementation of all three tiers as the model calls for, though most schools implement only universal school-wide elements
constraints: The trial trained schools only in the universal (Tier 1) school-wide supports, so causal inferences are limited to those elements
target_learners: Elementary school children in kindergarten through grade 2
target_learning_goals: Preventing disruptive and aggressive behavior
Enhancing school climate and social-emotional functioning
examples: 37 Maryland elementary schools were randomized to SWPBIS (21) or comparison (16), with SWPBIS schools receiving two-day summer training, annual boosters, and monthly on-site coaching
key_sources: Bradshaw, C. P., Waasdorp, T. E., & Leaf, P. J. (2015). Examining Variation in the Impact of School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports: Findings From a Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037630

article_title: Examining the Effects of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Student Outcomes: Results From a Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial in Elementary Schools
citation: Catherine P. Bradshaw, Mary M. Mitchell, & Philip J. Leaf. (2010). Examining the Effects of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Student Outcomes: Results From a Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial in Elementary Schools. Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions, 12(3), 133-148. https://doi.org/10.1177/1098300709334798
title: SWPBIS three-tiered prevention model
description: SWPBIS is a universal, schoolwide prevention strategy that "aims to alter school environments by creating improved systems and procedures that promote positive change in student behavior by targeting staff behaviors." It draws on behavioral, social learning, and organizational behavioral principles, and sits at the universal level of a three-tiered public health prevention model that also includes secondary (targeted/selective) and tertiary (individual/indicated) systems of support. The universal model is implemented through seven steps covering team formation, coaching, defined and taught expectations, reward systems, response to violations, and data-based decision making.
requirements: A SWPBIS team of 6 to 10 staff members and an administrator, an external behavioral support coach, and a formal data system for discipline data
constraints: This study examined only the universal SWPBIS model; targeted and indicated supports were not systematically implemented across trial schools
target_learners: all elementary school students (universal, schoolwide)
target_learning_goals: positive student behavior, reduced disruptive behavior, improved school climate
examples: The 21 trained schools formed internal SWPBIS teams, attended an initial 2-day summer training led by Dr. George Sugai, and held annual booster trainings

Examining the Effects of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Student Outcomes: Results From a Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial in Elementary Schools. citation: Catherine P. Bradshaw, Mary M. Mitchell, & Philip J. Leaf. (2010). Examining the Effects of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Student Outcomes: Results From a Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial in Elementary Schools. Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions, 12(3), 133-148. https://doi.org/10.1177/1098300709334798
title: School-Wide Information System (SWIS)
description: SWIS is "an Internet-based data entry and reporting system" used to collect and manage student discipline referral data by school staff. In this trial it was used to collect major (e.g., abusive language, fighting, lying) and minor (e.g., physical contact, disruption, property misuse) office referrals from the SWPBIS-trained schools in Years 1 through 4. SWIS use was conceptualized as part of the SWPBIS program, so ODR data were not available for baseline or comparison schools.
requirements: Staff training on completing an office discipline referral form consistent with SWIS to ensure consistent documentation across staff
constraints: The authors note researchers have questioned the validity of ODR data collected without formal training or a systematic data collection procedure
target_learners: school staff in SWPBIS-implementing schools
target_learning_goals: data-based decision making about discipline and program implementation
examples: The rate of major ODRs per 100 students per day in SWPBIS schools remained well below the national SWIS average of .34 to .37

article_title: The Impact of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Bullying and Peer Rejection
citation: Waasdorp TE, Bradshaw CP, Leaf PJ. (2012). The Impact of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Bullying and Peer Rejection: A Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial. Arch Pediatr Adolesc Med. 2012;166(2):149-156. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/archpediatrics/fullarticle/
title: SWPBIS: a noncurricular, universal, three-tiered schoolwide behavior support model
description: SWPBIS is described as "a noncurricular, universal prevention model that draws on behavioral, social learning, and organizational principles." A SWPBIS team establishes 3 to 5 positively stated schoolwide expectations that are posted, taught to all students and staff, and reinforced through praise and tangible rewards, with data on problem behaviors used to guide supervision and more intensive supports. It follows a 3-tiered public health prevention approach, layering targeted and indicated programs onto the universal model. In this trial, 21 elementary schools received training and coaching and reached high-fidelity implementation.
requirements: Internal SWPBIS teams attend initial training and annual booster training
On-site support from a trained behavior support coach
Data collection on student behaviors to monitor the universal program
constraints: In this trial intervention schools received training on the universal SWPBIS model only; more intensive selective and indicated tiers were not layered on
target_learners: Elementary school students (kindergarten through grade 5)
target_learning_goals: Positive social and classroom behavior
Reduced bullying and peer rejection
Improved school climate
examples: School teams established expectations such as "be respectful, responsible, and ready to learn," posted across settings and reinforced with tickets

article_title: Effects of a literary intervention on teachers’ monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students’ contributions
citation: Dammert, Y., Gasser, L., & Murphy, P. K. (2026). Effects of a literary intervention on teachers' monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students' contributions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09809-z
title: Swiss QT literary intervention package: nine mini-lessons, four literary-fiction books, literacy journals, and small-group discussions
description: The adapted intervention is a one-year language-arts program in which students were "instructed on how to identify various authentic questions, justify their claims, and collaboratively construct knowledge in discussions through nine mini-lessons". Students read and discussed four award-winning children's books in small groups across 11 literary discussions, kept literacy journals to prepare authentic questions and responses, and followed discussion rules establishing normative expectations for a dialogic culture. Teachers implemented the program with high fidelity, spending 34.07 hours versus a prescribed 32.92 hours.
requirements: Teacher professional development: two workshops plus three to four video-based coaching sessions
Heterogeneous small groups of three to seven students formed at the study's outset
constraints: The adaptation exclusively focuses on literary fiction with a moral-dilemma theme matching the assessment story
target_learners: Fourth- and fifth-grade students in German-speaking Swiss primary schools
target_learning_goals: Asking authentic questions
Justifying claims
Collaboratively constructing knowledge in discussion
examples: Books included The Very Persistent Gappers of Frip, Brown: My Alter Ego Is a Superhero, Rabbit & Bear: Attack of the Snack, and Balaclava Boy, with an average LIX score of 28.35 indicating low complexity.
key_sources: Dammert, Y., Gasser, L., & Murphy, P. K. (2026). Effects of a literary intervention on teachers' monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students' contributions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09809-z

article_title: Subtraction by addition in children with mathematical learning disabilities
citation: Peters, G., De Smedt, B., Torbeyns, J., Verschaffel, L., & Ghesquière, P. (2014). Subtraction by addition in children with mathematical learning disabilities. Learning and Instruction, 30, 1-8. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learn.instruc.2013.11.001
title: Strategy choice model: switching between direct subtraction and subtraction by addition predicted by the minimum of subtrahend and difference
description: The Switch-Model is a reaction-time regression model representing a strategy use pattern in which solvers switch between direct subtraction and subtraction by addition based on the relative magnitude of the subtrahend. Reaction times are predicted by min[D, S]: for problems with the subtrahend smaller than the difference, times increase with subtrahend size (direct subtraction expected); for problems with the subtrahend larger than the difference, times increase with difference size (subtraction by addition expected). It contrasts with the DS-Model (times predicted by subtrahend size) and the SBA-Model (times predicted by difference size).
requirements: Symbolically presented two-digit subtraction problems allowing classification by subtrahend size, difference size, and their minimum, with reaction time measurement
constraints: The article notes the non-verbal methods did not allow strategy identification at the item level
target_learners: children with mathematical learning disabilities
typically developing children
adults
target_learning_goals: understanding flexible strategy choice in mental multi-digit subtraction
examples: The model was fitted to mean reaction times of 32 subtraction-format problems, with the Switch-Model explaining 47 % of the variance
key_sources: Peters, G., De Smedt, B., Torbeyns, J., Verschaffel, L., & Ghesquière, P. (2014). Subtraction by addition in children with mathematical learning disabilities. Learning and Instruction, 30, 1-8. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2013.11.001

article_title: Exploring the impacts of interactions, social presence and emotional engagement on active collaborative learning in a social web-based environment
citation: Molinillo, S., Aguilar-Illescas, R., Anaya-Sánchez, R., & Vallespín-Arán, M. (2018). Exploring the impacts of interactions, social presence and emotional engagement on active collaborative learning in a social web-based environment. Computers & Education, 123, 41-52.
title: Research model of antecedents of active learning in social web-based collaborative learning
description: The article proposes and tests a parsimonious model in which "social presence, emotional engagement, teacher-student interactions and, to a lesser degree, student-student interactions (in that order)" act as antecedents of active learning in SWBCL. The model posits direct paths from social presence, teacher-student interaction and student-student interaction to active learning and emotional engagement, plus a path from emotional engagement to active learning. It was evaluated with PLS-SEM on survey data from 416 undergraduates.
requirements: Validated multi-item scales for the five constructs
Social web tools supporting interaction among group members
constraints: Causal relationships should be interpreted with caution because data are cross-sectional
Only four antecedents of active learning are considered
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: active collaborative learning in social web-based environments

title: Social web tool set (blogs, social networks, file sharing, forums, Skype, wikis) for collaborative case study work
description: The article describes a set of social web tools used by student groups: blogs used as learning diaries, social networks for synchronous and asynchronous communication, shared file storage, forums for coordination and announcements, Skype for voice and video calls, and wikis for collaborative write-up of the case analysis. Tools were accessed through the Moodle 2.5 platform over one semester.
requirements: Teachers instruct students in the use of the tools and establish objectives and guidance
constraints: Some very recent technologies were not included in the study

target_learning_goals: collaborative case analysis
knowledge co-production
communication and organization skills
examples: Each group managed a blog as a diary and used a wiki to collaboratively write up its case analysis

article_title: Effects of Semantic Web Based Learning on Pre-Service Teachers' ICT Learning Achievement and Satisfaction
citation: Karalar, H., & Korucu, A. T. (2016). Effects of Semantic Web Based Learning on Pre-service Teachers' ICT Learning Achievement and Satisfaction. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(8). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i8.1676
title: SWBL environment with OntoExcel ontology, pedagogical agent and learning object repository
description: The SWBL environment is a Semantic Web based learning system built around an ontology called OntoExcel developed in Protégé, a pedagogical agent, and a learning object repository. The agent reads the OntoExcel.OWL and LO.RDF files, answers queries through SPARQL, and lists prerequisite and posterior objectives with related learning objects. In the study it covered 5 spreadsheet topics with 74 learning objects created through PowerPoint videos with voice-over and PDF documents.
requirements: Internet access for learners to reach the content
learning objects and objectives defined in the ontology so the agent can list prerequisites
constraints: the article notes a dislike theme of necessity for Internet access, with one student unable to benefit due to no connection in the dormitory
target_learners: pre-service teachers in an ICT course
target_learning_goals: ICT spreadsheets objectives such as listing process priorities, writing and copying formulas
examples: The experimental group learned through PowerPoint videos of lectures with voice-over and PDF documents organized by objective, while the control group received the same lecture-based PowerPoint presentations as traditional teaching

article_title: Switch-On Reading: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Stephen Gorard, Beng Huat See, Nadia Siddiqui. (2014). Switch-on Reading: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/evaluation
title: Switch-on Reading: a 10-week one-to-one graded-book literacy intervention with running-record assessment
description: Switch-on Reading is an intensive 10-week literacy intervention delivered one to one by trained staff, mostly teaching assistants, in regular 20-minute sessions for Year 7 pupils below Level 4 English at Key Stage 2. It is inspired by Reading Recovery and "revolves around appropriately matched books that have been finely graded in bands and levels to provide small changes in challenge over time". Each session involves reading a familiar book, discussing content and visual material, reading new text with a running record, feedback, and introducing a new book, with pupils reading from four graded books per session.
requirements: Staff require two days of training in the approach, running-record use and the protocol, plus ongoing monitoring and support to adhere to the developer's schedule
constraints: Implementation challenges include timetabling and availability of age-appropriate texts; some staff tend to stray from the explicit schedule
target_learners: Year 7 pupils at the primary-secondary transition who have not achieved Level 4 English at Key Stage 2
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and fluency; functional literacy for weak readers
examples: In the trial, 83 staff from 19 schools were trained and 71 delivered the intervention; each staff member looked after no more than four pupils, and error inventories from the running record determined which book set followed next
key_sources: Stephen Gorard, Beng Huat See, Nadia Siddiqui. (2014). Switch-on Reading: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/evaluation

article_title: Switch-On Effectiveness Trial: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Rakhee Patel, Nico Jabin, Loraine Bussard, Javiera Cartagena, Sarah Haywood and Michael Lumpkin. (2017). Switch-on Effectiveness Trial. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/our-work/projects/switch-on-effectiveness-trial/
title: Switch-on intensive targeted literacy intervention
description: Switch-on is "an intensive, targeted literacy intervention that aims to improve the reading skills of pupils who are struggling with literacy", delivered by specially trained Teaching Assistants in daily 20-minute sessions over a ten-week period. Two versions were trialled: Switch-on Reading (daily reading sessions) and Switch-on Reading and Writing (alternating writing and reading sessions). Sessions revise familiar texts, introduce new texts and vocabulary, practise phonics, and work on comprehension, with TAs using Running Records to monitor progress and tailor prompts.
requirements: Delivery by trained TAs with a school co-ordinator from the senior management team
A pack of 180 reading books across 30 reading levels and 15 colour bands
TA training of 1.5 days for Switch-on Reading and 2.5 days for Switch-on Reading and Writing
constraints: Aimed at Year 3 pupils working below age-related expectations at the end of Key Stage 1 without a high level of special needs
target_learners: Year 3 pupils (aged seven and eight) struggling with literacy
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and word recognition
Writing skills (Switch-on Reading and Writing version)
examples: In the trial, each TA worked with between two and four pupils, and 999 pupils across 184 schools participated over the 2015/2016 academic year
key_sources: Rakhee Patel, Nico Jabin, Loraine Bussard, Javiera Cartagena, Sarah Haywood and Michael Lumpkin. (2017). Switch-on Effectiveness Trial. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/our-work/projects/switch-on-effectiveness-trial/

article_title: Switch-On Effectiveness Trial: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Rakhee Patel, Nico Jabin, Loraine Bussard, Javiera Cartagena, Sarah Haywood and Michael Lumpkin. (2017). Switch-on Effectiveness Trial. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/our-work/projects/switch-on-effectiveness-trial/
title: Switch-on theoretical framework: zone of proximal development and the simple view of reading
description: The Switch-on manual and training grounded the intervention in two frameworks. Vygotsky's "theory of the zone of proximal development, which draws a distinction between what a learner can do independently and with help from an adult or more competent peer" underpins the one-to-one supported delivery. The "simple view of reading", which "distinguishes between language comprehension processes and word recognition skills and demonstrates that both are essential for effective reading", informed session content covering both comprehension and phonics. The training also explained the rationale for re-reading familiar books to build confidence and fluency.
requirements: TAs trained in these frameworks through the intervention manual and accompanying training
constraints: Framework as presented in the Switch-on training manual; the trial did not independently test the theoretical account
target_learners: Year 3 pupils working below age-related expectations in literacy
target_learning_goals: Reading strategies, confidence, fluency and comprehension
examples: Sessions incorporated revision of familiar texts, new text introduction, phonics practice, and comprehension questions and discussions
key_sources: Rakhee Patel, Nico Jabin, Loraine Bussard, Javiera Cartagena, Sarah Haywood and Michael Lumpkin. (2017). Switch-on Effectiveness Trial. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/our-work/projects/switch-on-effectiveness-trial/

article_title: Using Argument-Based Science Inquiry to Improve Science Achievement for Students with Disabilities in Inclusive Classrooms
citation: Jonte C. Taylor, Ching-mei Tseng, Brian Hand, Angelique Murillo, William Therrien. (2018). Using Argument-based Science Inquiry to Improve Science Achievement for Students with Disabilities in Inclusive Classrooms. Journal of Science Education for Students with Disabilities, Vol. 21, No. 1. http://scholarworks.rit.edu/jsesd/vol21/iss1/2
title: SWH teacher and student templates scaffolding argument-based inquiry
description: The SWH uses paired teacher and student templates to scaffold teaching and learning during science instruction (Table 1). The teacher template guides teachers through phases from pre-laboratory activities through four negotiations phases to post-instruction exploration, while the student template walks students through beginning ideas, questions, tests, observations, claims, evidence, reading, reflection, and writing. "Using the templates, students develop questions, make claims, and provide evidence to support or reject claims." Teachers were taught to use the templates as pedagogical support but could adjust the sequence for classroom needs.
requirements: Teachers are directed to use the templates to construct lessons and instructional activities
constraints: Teachers were encouraged to adjust the template sequence for their classroom needs
target_learners: Elementary students with IEPs in inclusive science classrooms
target_learning_goals: Understanding the scientific process
Making claims supported by evidence
examples: The student template pairs prompts such as 'What can I claim?' with teacher-template phases such as 'Negotiations phase I - writing personal meanings for laboratory activity'

Using Argument-based Science Inquiry to Improve Science Achievement for Students with Disabilities in Inclusive Classrooms. article_title: Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Support Practices: Review of Studies in the "Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions"
citation: Öğülmüş, K., & Vuran, S. (2016). Schoolwide positive behavioral interventions and support practices: Review of studies in the Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 16, 1693–1710. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2016.5.0264
title: SWPBIS is organized around three major themes: prevention, multi-tiered support, and data-based decision making
description: The article defines SWPBIS as a framework whose processes are "arranged around three major themes: Prevention, Multi-Tiered Support, and Data-based Decision Making." Prevention involves describing and teaching behavioral expectations, approving and rewarding appropriate behavior, and building a regular continuation of outcomes for problem behavior. The framework aims to build a positive social atmosphere where expectations are foreseeable, directly taught, constantly approved, and actively observed.
requirements: Describing and teaching basic behavioral expectations
Approving and awarding appropriate behavior
Building a regular continuation of outcomes for problem behavior
target_learners: all students in a school
target_learning_goals: reduce problem behavior
improve school climate and academic achievement
examples: Over 9,000 US schools are reported as implementing SWPBIS to decrease disruptive behavior problems
key_sources: Öğülmüş, K., & Vuran, S. (2016). Schoolwide positive behavioral interventions and support practices: Review of studies in the Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 16, 1693–1710. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2016.5.0264

article_title: Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Support Practices: Review of Studies in the "Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions"
citation: Öğülmüş, K., & Vuran, S. (2016). Schoolwide positive behavioral interventions and support practices: Review of studies in the Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 16, 1693–1710. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2016.5.0264
title: Three-tiered prevention continuum of positive behavior support (primary, secondary, tertiary)
description: The article presents a three-tiered prevention continuum in which primary prevention is schoolwide implementation with defined and taught behavioral expectations, rewards, and a continuum of consequences; secondary prevention adds direct instruction on organization, social interaction, and academic skills with increased structure and feedback; tertiary prevention uses strengths-based and functional behavioral assessment, applied behavior analysis, intensive instruction, and self-management. Each tier pairs student-focused practices with faculty- and staff-focused systems such as team-based implementation and use of fidelity data.
requirements: Team-based implementation and administrative commitment at the primary tier
Progress monitoring and regular team meetings at the secondary tier
Access to behavioral expertise at the tertiary tier

article_title: Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Support Practices: Review of Studies in the "Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions"

title: Seven key features of schoolwide positive behavior support
description: The article reports that Horner, Todd, Lewis-Palmer, Irvin, Sugai, and Boland (2004) explained seven key features of schoolwide positive behavior support: describing 3-5 expectations for appropriate behavior schoolwide; actively having all students learn those expectations; observing and approving students when they engage in expected behavior; correcting problem behaviors with a regularly administered continuum of outcomes; collecting and using behavior data for decision-making; obtaining leadership from a director who organizes a team; and getting district-level support.
requirements: A director who organizes a team to establish, carry out, and administer the schoolwide behavior support attempt
District-level support including education in schoolwide behavior support applications
target_learners: all students in a school

title: SW-PBIS implementation should be integrated with other school reform initiatives to improve academic outcomes
description: The authors recommend layering more intensive interventions within the school-wide framework and integrating SW-PBIS with other approaches intended to promote student learning. As they conclude, "SW-PBIS may engender greater educational benefits in schools if it is integrated with other approaches intended to promote student learning." This recommendation follows directly from the study's null findings on both academic and behavioral outcomes.
requirements: SW-PBIS must first be implemented as a school-wide framework before more intensive academic interventions can be layered on
constraints: Based on null findings in a single-state quasi-experimental study with school-level outcomes over three years

positive student behavior

article_title: Adapting the one minute preceptor model to a Swedish context - clinical tutors' experiences of its usage in primary health care.
citation: Rothlind E, Salminen H, Rolfhamre K, Karlgren K, Toth-Pal E. (2025). Adapting the one minute preceptor model to a Swedish context – clinical tutors’ experiences of its usage in primary health care. Scandinavian Journal of Primary Health Care. https://doi.org/10.1080/02813432.2025.2508370
title: Adapted Swedish OMP workshop: a 1.5-hour interprofessional training with role-play, example video and laminated micro-skill cards
description: A 1.5-hour formal training session for physician and nurse clinical tutors in primary care, including a PowerPoint presentation on OMP key elements, an example video, and a role-play activity practised in pairs without an audience. The five micro-skills were translated into Swedish and adapted: 'Correct mistakes' was replaced with 'feedforward', and 'rule of thumb' was chosen instead of 'general rules' to "incorporate experience-based knowledge". Laminated cards outlining the micro-skills and example questions were provided, with 'teach rule of thumb' placed last to reinforce feedforward.
requirements: Ongoing tutorship of medical (year three or higher) or nursing (year two or higher) students at PHC centres with 8000 or more registered patients
Material adapted for both physicians and nurses
constraints: Role plays practised in pairs without an audience because acting in front of others was a concern raised in needs assessment interviews
target_learners: Clinical tutors (physicians and nurses) in primary health care
target_learning_goals: Clinical tutoring skills including feedback, feedforward and eliciting student clinical reasoning
examples: 93 tutors at 11 PHC centres attended the workshops; workshop components were rated 4.44 (PowerPoint), 4.37 (video) and 4.25 (role play) on a five-point scale

title: Linked Swedish nationwide register dataset on school performance and family background (829,787 children born 1994–2004)
description: A linked nationwide register dataset built from the National School Register, Inpatient and Outpatient Registers, Total Population Register, Multi-Generation Register, and the Longitudinal Integration Database for Health Insurance and Labor Market Studies, covering "829,787 children born 1994–2004". Records were linked via the unique 10-digit identification number assigned to all Swedish residents and pseudonymised by serial number. Outcomes were ninth-grade totals from 0 to 320 across 16 subjects, assessed over 11 graduation years (2010–2020).
requirements: Swedish nationwide register linkage via the unique 10-digit identification number
approval by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority
constraints: datasets not readily shareable due to legal concerns
parental mental disorder measured only from 2001 onward and during compulsory school years
target_learners: compulsory-school (ninth grade) students in Sweden
target_learning_goals: school performance measured as ninth-grade total scores across 16 subjects
examples: The study derived descriptive statistics by graduation year and ran sex-stratified linear mixed models with a sibling random effect for familial clustering.

article_title: Effect of hands-on interprofessional simulation training for local emergencies in Scotland: the THISTLE stepped-wedge design randomised controlled trial.
citation: Lenguerrand Erik, Winter Cathy, Siassakos Dimitrios, MacLennan Graeme, Innes Karen, Lynch Pauline, Cameron Alan, Crofts Joanna, McDonald Alison, McCormack Kirsty, Forrest Mark, Norrie John, Bhattacharya Siladitya, Draycott Tim. (2020). Effect of hands-on interprofessional simulation training for local emergencies in Scotland: the THISTLE stepped-wedge design randomised controlled trial. BMJ Quality & Safety 29(2):122-134. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjqs-2018-008625
title: Stepped-wedge trials of training interventions should include a feasibility stage, a parallel process evaluation, and measurement of the proportion of staff trained
description: The authors recommend that future stepped-wedge trials evaluating training interventions plan for implementation difficulty from the outset. They state that "future SW-RCT studies should consider a feasibility stage and a parallel process evaluation" to explore barriers and facilitators to randomisation and implementation, and that such trials "should allocate resources to enable the measurement of the proportion of staff trained", since intervention penetration could not be assessed in THISTLE.
requirements: Resources to measure the cumulative proportion of staff trained at each unit over the study period
constraints: The theoretical savings in time, resources and staffing offered by the SW-RCT design may be limited for interventions requiring behavioural change or authentic implementation in busy health systems
target_learners: Maternity unit staff (midwives, obstetricians, anaesthetists) undergoing multiprofessional emergency training
target_learning_goals: Management of intrapartum emergencies and team-working in maternity care
examples: In THISTLE, units could not provide baseline staffing numbers so the cumulative proportion of staff trained could not be derived, and only limited process data were collected to reduce workload on clinical staff.
